hints: Focus on what changes when the C=C double bond opens up to form the long polymer chain.
Remember ethene has a double bond with trigonal planar carbons, while poly(ethene) has only single bonds with tetrahedral carbons.
Think about which type of covalent bond is found in every single and every double bond, so it must survive polymerisation.
walkthrough:
**Draw ethene in your mind**

Think of ethene as $\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}_2$ with a C=C double bond. Each carbon is $sp^2$ hybridised, trigonal planar, with bond angles of about $120^{\circ}$.

$$\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}_2 : \text{ 1 } \sigma + \text{ 1 } \pi \text{ in C=C}$$

**Draw poly(ethene) in your mind**

During addition polymerisation the $\pi$ bond breaks and each ethene links by single bonds to make $\text{-(CH}_2\text{-CH}_2\text{)-}_n$. Each carbon is now $sp^3$ hybridised, tetrahedral, with bond angles of $109.5^{\circ}$.

$$\text{-(CH}_2\text{-CH}_2\text{)-}_n : \text{ only } \sigma \text{ bonds}$$

**Find what is common**

Every covalent bond starts with a $\sigma$ bond. Ethene has $\sigma$ bonds (C-H and C-C) plus one $\pi$ bond, and poly(ethene) has only $\sigma$ bonds (C-H and C-C). So $\sigma$ covalent bonds are present in both.

options.A: Incorrect. $109.5^{\circ}$ is the tetrahedral angle found in poly(ethene) where carbons are $sp^3$. Ethene has trigonal planar carbons with angles of about $120^{\circ}$, so this is not common to both.
options.B: Incorrect. Ethene has a $\pi$ bond as part of its C=C double bond. This $\pi$ bond is broken during polymerisation to form new C-C $\sigma$ bonds, so poly(ethene) contains no $\pi$ bonds.
options.C: Correct. Both molecules contain many $\sigma$ covalent bonds. Ethene has $\sigma$ C-H and C-C bonds plus a $\pi$ bond, while poly(ethene) has only $\sigma$ C-H and C-C bonds. The $\sigma$ framework is present in both.
options.D: Incorrect. $sp^3$ orbitals are only in poly(ethene) where each carbon forms four $\sigma$ bonds. Ethene uses $sp^2$ orbitals to give its planar shape and to leave a p orbital for the $\pi$ bond.
